references.text: When Lot was led out of Sodom, he was told: 'Flee for your life! Do not look back' (Gen 19:17). Jesus uses the destruction of Sodom precisely as a type of the coming judgment (v. 29), and the warning not to turn back has a direct parallel to Lot's flight.
Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Gen 19:26). Jesus mentions her explicitly in the next verse (Luke 17:32) as a warning example of what happens to those who turn back.

In Jesus' eschatological discourse in Matt 24:17-18, he gives the same warning: whoever is on the roof should not go down to get anything from the house, and whoever is in the field should not turn back to get their cloak. This is a close parallel to Luke's version.

Also in Mark 13:15-16, there is the same warning that whoever is on the roof should not go down or enter to get anything, and whoever is in the field should not turn back. Mark's version is linked to the destruction of Jerusalem.

Jesus says in Luke 9:62 that 'no one who puts their hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.' The theme of not turning back (μὴ ἐπιστρεψάτω εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω) has a thematic connection to this statement about wholehearted discipleship.
Paul writes in Phil 3:13-14 about forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead. It shares the thematic motif of not turning back to what one has left, but pressing on.

The immediate context in Luke 17:32-33 reinforces the warning: 'Remember Lot's wife!' and 'Whoever tries to save their life will lose it.' Turning back to rescue one's possessions is an expression of clinging to this life rather than following God's way of salvation.
